cpi.label: Consumer prices (CPI)
cpi.what: How much more a typical household's shopping basket costs than a year ago. The most-quoted inflation number.
cpi.why: Inflation eats into what wages and savings can buy. The Federal Reserve aims for 2% a year.
cpi.rule: Healthy: at or under 2.5% (near the Fed's 2% goal). Watch: 2.5% to 3.5%. Strained: over 3.5%.

core_cpi.label: Core CPI (no food or energy)
core_cpi.what: Consumer prices leaving out food and energy, which swing a lot from month to month.
core_cpi.why: Shows the underlying trend in prices. Economists watch it to see if inflation is sticking.
core_cpi.rule: Healthy: at or under 2.5% (near the Fed's 2% goal). Watch: 2.5% to 3.5%. Strained: over 3.5%.

pce.label: PCE prices
pce.what: The Commerce Department's price measure, built from what people actually spend. Wider than CPI.
pce.why: The Fed's official 2% target is set on this measure.
pce.rule: Healthy: at or under 2.5% (near the Fed's 2% goal). Watch: 2.5% to 3.5%. Strained: over 3.5%.

core_pce.label: Core PCE (the Fed's favorite)
core_pce.what: PCE prices leaving out food and energy.
core_pce.why: The Fed's preferred gauge of underlying inflation when it sets interest rates.
core_pce.rule: Healthy: at or under 2.5% (near the Fed's 2% goal). Watch: 2.5% to 3.5%. Strained: over 3.5%.

shelter.label: Shelter (rent and housing costs)
shelter.what: The rent and owner-housing part of CPI, the biggest single piece of the basket.
shelter.why: Housing is the largest bill for most households, and it changes slowly, so it often keeps CPI high after other prices cool.

food.label: Food prices
food.why: The prices people notice most every week.

energy.label: Energy prices
energy.why: Energy is volatile and feeds into the cost of nearly everything else.

wages.label: Average hourly pay
wages.what: How much average hourly earnings of private-sector workers have grown over the past year.
wages.why: Pay growing faster than prices means paychecks are buying more. Slower means they are buying less.
wages.rule: Healthy: pay growth at or above consumer-price inflation (paychecks keep up). Watch: up to 1 point below. Strained: more than 1 point below.

breakeven.label: Market's 10-year inflation expectation
breakeven.what: What bond investors are pricing in for average yearly inflation over the next 10 years (the gap between regular and inflation-protected Treasury yields).
breakeven.why: Shows whether markets trust the Fed to keep inflation near target.

mich.label: Consumers' expected inflation (next 12 months)
mich.what: What households surveyed by the University of Michigan expect prices to do over the next year.
mich.why: Expectations can feed on themselves: if people expect higher prices, they ask for higher pay and raise prices.

ffr.label: Fed funds rate
ffr.what: The rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Federal Reserve's main policy lever.
ffr.why: It sets the cost of borrowing across the economy: mortgages, credit cards, business loans, and what savings accounts pay.

y3m.label: 3-month Treasury yield
y3m.what: What the US government pays to borrow for three months.
y3m.why: Tracks where markets expect the Fed's rate to be soon.

y2.label: 2-year Treasury yield
y2.what: What the US government pays to borrow for two years.
y2.why: The market's best guess at the Fed's path. It moves first when expectations change.

y10.label: 10-year Treasury yield
y10.what: What the US government pays to borrow for ten years. The benchmark for mortgages and long-term loans.
y10.why: When it rises, borrowing gets more expensive, and stocks (especially growth stocks) face a higher bar.
y10.rule: Healthy: under 4%. Watch: 4% to 5%. Strained: over 5% (borrowing is expensive across the economy).

y30.label: 30-year Treasury yield
y30.what: What the US government pays to borrow for thirty years.
y30.why: The longest-term price of money. Rising long yields can signal worries about inflation or government debt.

real10.label: 10-year real yield
real10.what: The 10-year yield after removing expected inflation (TIPS yield).
real10.why: The true cost of long-term money. High real yields squeeze borrowers and pull money out of stocks and gold.

t10y2y.label: Yield curve: 10-year minus 2-year
t10y2y.what: The gap between the 10-year and 2-year yields. Normally positive, because lenders want more for lending longer.
t10y2y.why: When it falls below zero (an 'inverted' curve), short-term money pays more than long-term, which has often come before recessions.
t10y2y.rule: Healthy: more than 0.25 points above zero. Watch: within 0.25 of zero. Strained: inverted by more than 0.25.

t10y3m.label: Yield curve: 10-year minus 3-month
t10y3m.what: The gap between the 10-year and 3-month yields. The version many researchers (including the New York Fed) use.
t10y3m.why: Inversions of this gap have a strong record of coming before US recessions, though with a lag of many months and no guarantee.
t10y3m.rule: Healthy: more than 0.25 points above zero. Watch: within 0.25 of zero. Strained: inverted by more than 0.25.

mortgage.label: 30-year mortgage rate
mortgage.what: The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage (Freddie Mac survey).
mortgage.why: Sets monthly payments for home buyers and drives the housing market.

hy.label: Junk-bond spread
hy.what: How much extra interest risky ('high-yield') companies pay over Treasuries.
hy.why: A widening spread means lenders are getting nervous about companies' ability to repay. A narrow one means they are relaxed.
hy.rule: Healthy: under 4 points. Watch: 4 to 6. Strained: over 6 (lenders are demanding a lot extra).

unrate.label: Unemployment rate
unrate.what: The share of people in the labor force who want a job and can't find one.
unrate.why: The simplest read on whether people who want work can get it.
unrate.rule: Healthy: 4.5% or less. Watch: 4.5% to 5.5%. Strained: over 5.5%.

u6.label: Broad unemployment (U-6)
u6.what: Counts the unemployed plus discouraged workers and people stuck in part-time work who want full-time.
u6.why: A fuller picture of slack in the job market than the headline rate.

payrolls.label: Jobs added per month
payrolls.what: How many jobs the economy added (or lost) in the latest month, from the employer survey.
payrolls.why: The headline jobs report. Steady gains mean employers are still hiring.
payrolls.rule: Based on the 3-month average. Healthy: at least 100,000 jobs a month. Watch: 0 to 100,000. Strained: losing jobs.

claims.label: Jobless claims (4-week average)
claims.what: New applications for unemployment benefits each week, averaged over four weeks.
claims.why: The fastest signal of layoffs. A sustained rise is often the first sign that the job market is turning.
claims.rule: Healthy: under 250,000 a week. Watch: 250,000 to 300,000. Strained: over 300,000.

openings.label: Job openings
openings.what: How many jobs employers are trying to fill (JOLTS survey).
openings.why: More openings than unemployed people means workers have leverage; falling openings show hiring is cooling.

lfpr.label: Labor force participation
lfpr.what: The share of adults who are working or looking for work.
lfpr.why: Shows how much of the population is in the workforce, which depends on aging, health and confidence in finding work.

sahm.label: Sahm rule recession indicator
sahm.what: Compares the recent unemployment rate with its lowest level of the past year. Hitting 0.5 points has signaled the start of every US recession since 1970.
sahm.why: A rule-of-thumb alarm built from unemployment alone. It has been right on timing so far, but it is a rule, not a law.
sahm.rule: Healthy: under 0.3. Watch: 0.3 to 0.5. Strained: 0.5 or more (the recession signal).

gdp.label: Economic growth (real GDP)
gdp.what: How fast the economy grew in the latest quarter, as an annualized rate after inflation.
gdp.why: The broadest measure of whether the economy is expanding or shrinking. Two negative quarters in a row is the popular definition of a recession.
gdp.rule: Healthy: growing at 2% or faster. Watch: 0% to 2%. Strained: shrinking.

indpro.label: Industrial production
indpro.what: Output of factories, mines and utilities compared with a year ago.
indpro.why: A narrower but timely read on the goods side of the economy.
indpro.rule: Healthy: output up 1% or more on a year. Watch: between -1% and +1%. Strained: down more than 1%.

retail.label: Retail sales
retail.what: Spending in stores and online compared with a year ago (not adjusted for inflation).
retail.why: Consumers drive about two-thirds of the US economy. Remember that inflation inflates this number.

sentiment.label: Consumer sentiment
sentiment.what: A University of Michigan survey of how households feel about their finances and the economy.
sentiment.why: Confidence can lead spending. It is a mood measure and often swings with prices and politics.

vix.label: Market fear gauge (VIX)
vix.what: How much stock-market swing options traders are pricing in over the next 30 days.
vix.why: Low means calm; spikes come with sell-offs.
vix.rule: Healthy: under 20. Watch: 20 to 30. Strained: over 30.

nfci.label: Financial conditions (Chicago Fed)
nfci.what: A weekly index of how easy or hard it is to get credit and finance things. Zero is the long-run average.
nfci.why: Positive means tighter than average (money is harder to get); negative means looser.
nfci.rule: Healthy: below zero (looser than average). Watch: 0 to 0.5. Strained: above 0.5 (tight).

stlfsi.label: Financial stress (St. Louis Fed)
stlfsi.what: A weekly index built from 18 market measures such as interest rates, yield gaps and volatility. Zero is the long-run average.
stlfsi.why: Positive means more stress than normal in financial markets.
stlfsi.rule: Healthy: below zero (looser than average). Watch: 0 to 0.5. Strained: above 0.5 (tight).

source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), using data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, Federal Reserve Board, Treasury, University of Michigan, Freddie Mac and ICE
